source.title: Stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system: present status and open problems

accepted.question_text: Do there exist stationary axisymmetric solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system that are genuinely far from spherical symmetry in both spatial density and net angular momentum, including regular solutions that contain ergoregions, and can such solutions be established analytically rather than only through perturbations of known nearly spherical states?

evidence.quote: A common feature of the existence results is that the solutions are obtained as perturbations of known solutions. Hence solutions which are far-from-spherically-symmetric in the sense of spatial density and net angular mo- mentum –in particular, solutions containing ergoregions– are not covered by these results. Accordingly, there is extensive room for analytic progress on the existence of stationary solutions.

accepted.question_text: Can one prove that the fixed-point map underlying the numerical iteration scheme for stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions actually has a fixed point in the axially symmetric setting, so that the numerically generated stationary solutions are supported by a rigorous existence argument?

evidence.quote: Hence the exact problem that is solved is a priori not known, it is determined once K(ρ∗) is known. It is an open problem to show that the map T has a fixed point.

Similar fixed point problems, based on the same strategy, can be formu- lated for several related systems; e.g. the spherically symmetric Einstein- Vlasov system and the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system. It is an open problem in each case to show the existence of a fixed point.

accepted.question_text: Can regular stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions with ergoregions be constructed beyond the currently observed regime, in particular with total angular momentum satisfying |J| < M^2 or by using ansatz families different from the step-function choice used in existing computations?

evidence.quote: Perhaps a different nu- merical scheme will be more successful in finding solutions with ergoregions and with |J | < M2.

Given this, one might speculate that the solutions obtained in [44] were not relativistic enough to contain ergoregions. It would be interesting to look for ergoregions in families of solutions obtained from other (non-step function) ansatzes.

accepted.question_text: Is a quasistationary transition from regular stationary axisymmetric Einstein-Vlasov solutions to a black hole, specifically an extremal Kerr black hole, actually possible, or is there instead a strict upper bound on the compactness parameter Γ below 1 or an unavoidable drift toward the thin-ring limit as the cutoff energy is decreased?

evidence.quote: With more computational effort and resolution can one continue this bisection search and reach all the way to a black hole solution? It is not clear that the answer to this question is affirmative.
Hence, from this discussion an essential question arises: is a transition of stationary solutions to black hole solutions possible?

Perhaps there is a maximum value of the compactness parameter Γ which is strictly below one as in the spherically symmetric case. Perhaps solutions necessarily approach the thin ring limit when E0 is successively decreased independently of the value of L0.

accepted.question_text: Can one rigorously establish the existence and limiting geometry of the thin-ring regime for rotating toroidal Einstein-Vlasov solutions, where the matter distribution becomes nearly Dirac-concentrated and the local geometry appears conical as in a cosmic-string-like limit?

evidence.quote: The thin-ring limit discussed in the section above has interesting properties of its own.
Due to the near Dirac nature of the spatial matter distribution in this limit, proving existence of such solutions may be analytically tractable.
Perhaps a similar study is possible in the axially symmetric case by utilizing the Dirac nature of the thin ring solutions.

accepted.question_text: Can the Einstein-Vlasov system admit three-dimensional stationary solutions that genuinely resemble realistic disk galaxies, and if so, do surrounding dark-matter-halo-type configurations improve numerical convergence and help produce the pronounced flattening seen in observations?

evidence.quote: We find it to be a central open problem to answer the question whether or not it is possible to ob- tain solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system which resemble realistic disk galaxies.
It is a question of great importance to investigate if such halos surrounding disk- like solutions do improve the convergence of the numerical algorithm.
To our knowl- edge this has not been investigated for the Einstein-Vlasov system and we find it to be an essential open problem.

accepted.question_text: Which nontrivial combinations of ansatz functions produce convergent composite stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions, and when such composite solutions exist, do they reproduce the morphologies of composite astrophysical systems observed in nature?

evidence.quote: An open issue is to understand which combinations of ansatz functions give rise to composite solutions and to find out if these solutions resemble the morphology of composite objects found in nature.

accepted.question_text: Do compactly supported massless axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov solutions exist, meaning solutions for which the particle density vanishes outside a compact region so that the matter configuration could in principle be matched to a vacuum exterior, and would such solutions realize an axisymmetric analogue of Wheeler-style geon configurations?

evidence.quote: Hence, the crucial question is whether or not massless axially symmetric solutions can be constructed such that the density function vanishes outside a compact set. If so, it would be possible to glue the solution to a vacuum solution –although no explicit vacuum solution exists as in the spherically symmetric case.
Hence, the question whether or not axially symmetric solutions of the massless Einstein-Vlasov system exist is closely related to the existence of Wheeler’s original conception of geons.

accepted.question_text: Can one construct general axially symmetric self-gravitating Einstein-Vlasov configurations around a central black hole, beyond perturbative or small-matter bifurcation regimes near vacuum or Kerr backgrounds?

evidence.quote: By the nature of the proof however, the matter must be small (close to vacuum), and it remains an open problem to find general axially symmetric self-gravitating solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system with a central black hole.

accepted.question_text: What is the structure of general axisymmetric solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov-Maxwell system when one goes beyond perturbative regimes with restricted angular momentum and weak gravitational field?

evidence.quote: The total angular momentum and the strength of the gravitational field are still restricted, and an understand- ing of general solutions to the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov-Maxwell system is lacking.

accepted.question_text: Are the highly compact stationary axisymmetric Einstein-Vlasov solutions found numerically stable under time evolution, and if they are to be tested dynamically, how can the extremely high spatial resolution needed to construct those stationary states be carried into an evolution code in a computationally feasible way?
accepted.context_brief: stability and evolution of compact states

evidence.quote: It is an outstanding problem to determine whether or not these solutions are stable.
How can the high resolution needed for the stationary solution be carried over to the evolution problem to make a simulation practically feasible?

Rewrote the central-black-hole discussion into a general existence question beyond small-matter perturbative constructions.
Rewrote the Einstein-Vlasov-Maxwell extension into a standalone question about the non-perturbative axisymmetric regime.
